query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an optimized laser shock peening treatment to eutectic high-entropy alloys will modify the internal lamellar-colony boundaries by inducing localized compressive residual stresses and nanostructural improvements, which will suppress microcrack initiation and propagation, thereby simultaneously enhancing room-temperature tensile strength and ductility compared to the unmodified material.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloys featuring dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that serve as microcrack nucleation sites during room-temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: A targeted post-processing treatment using optimized laser shock peening (or analogous shot peening) to engineer the internal interfaces of the lamellar colonies.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation conditions on as-cast or conventionally processed eutectic high-entropy alloy specimens.
generation.structural_mediator: Modified internal boundaries exhibiting compressive residual stresses and improved nanostructural cohesion that resist microcrack formation.
generation.mechanism: Laser shock peening induces compressive residual stresses at the internal colony boundaries and refines their microstructure, reducing stress concentrations and delaying or preventing the nucleation and propagation of microcracks under tensile load, which in turn enhances both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated baseline, specimens treated with laser shock peening will show higher tensile strength and increased tensile ductility, with delayed onset and reduced density of microcracks during deformation.
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic high-entropy alloys with dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibit microcrack initiation at internal boundaries under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected under controlled processing conditions for specific alloy compositions; excessively high or low peening intensities or processing deviations may not yield the desired interfacial modifications and could even be detrimental to mechanical properties.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvement in strength and ductility and the optimal laser shock peening parameters remain uncertain and require systematic experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical eutectic high-entropy alloy specimens. Apply the optimized laser shock peening treatment to the experimental group while keeping the control group untreated. Subject both groups to standardized room-temperature tensile tests.
measurements: Fracture surface and microcrack density analysis via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the laser shock peened specimens do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility, or if microcrack initiation and propagation patterns are similar to those of the untreated controls.

decision.trend: Early work (PMC4145285) introduced eutectic high‐entropy alloys with a naturally formed lamellar (fcc/B2) dual-phase structure that already provided an attractive baseline for strength and ductility. Later studies (PMC5818523, PMC6353877, PMC6687781) employed advanced thermomechanical processing (e.g., cryo-rolling, hybrid-rolling, and annealing) to refine the lamellar morphology and develop a hierarchical microstructure. These interventions improved strength by reducing grain size and creating dual heterogeneities but left the high density of internal colony interfaces insufficiently engineered, so that microcrack nucleation at these boundaries still limits room‐temperature ductility.
decision.unsolved: The key unsolved issue is the inherent vulnerability of the numerous internal (colony) boundaries within the lamellar microstructure; these boundaries remain preferential sites for microcrack initiation during tensile deformation and, despite prior microstructural refinements, have not been adequately modified to arrest crack propagation without sacrificing strength.
decision.lever: Application of a targeted post‐processing treatment—such as laser shock peening (or analogous shot peening) optimized to induce compressive residual stresses and locally modify the interfacial structure of the lamellar boundaries
decision.why: Following the trend of refining overall microstructure via thermomechanical treatments, the next logical step is to directly address the internal interfaces. By engineering the boundaries through a surface/interface treatment, one can improve the cohesive strength and toughness of those critical regions. The induced compressive residual stress and potential interfacial nanostructural modification should suppress microcrack initiation and hinder propagation, thereby enhancing both room‐temperature tensile strength and ductility relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline. An experiment contrasting tensile responses and fracture behaviors of treated versus untreated specimens would provide a clear falsification test of this hypothesis.
